evidence.quote:
In course of time, however, the thing got ground, the experiment was
made, and they lighted up Pall Mall.
evidence.paraphrase: Gas lighting is introduced and installed in Pall Mall, marking a technological shift.

evidence.quote:
I foresee in
this," he says, "the breaking up of our profession.  There
s no more
going the rounds to trim by daylight
evidence.paraphrase: A lamplighter predicts that gas lighting will destroy the lamplighting profession.

evidence.quote:
till one night he hung himself on a lamp-iron in Saint Martin
s
Lane, and there was an end of _him_.
evidence.paraphrase: Distressed by the coming of gas lighting, Tom's uncle goes mad and takes his own life.

evidence.quote:
I read what
s going to happen, in the stars.
evidence.paraphrase: The old gentleman claims he can read future events in the stars.

evidence.quote:
I have consulted the book of Fate
with rare and wonderful success.  I am versed in the great sciences of
astrology and astronomy.  In my house here, I have every description of
apparatus for observing the course and motion of the planets.
evidence.paraphrase: The old gentleman describes his astrological/astronomical practice and apparatus for observing the planets.

evidence.quote:
I
m in search of the
philosopher
s stone.  I have very nearly found it
not quite.  It turns
everything to gold; that
s its property.
evidence.paraphrase: The old gentleman explains he is seeking the philosopher's stone that turns everything to gold.

evidence.quote:
filled with all
manner of bottles, globes, books, telescopes, crocodiles, alligators, and
other scientific instruments of every kind.  In the centre of this room
was a stove or furnace, with what Tom called a pot, but which in my
opinion was a crucible, in full boil.
evidence.paraphrase: Description of a laboratory full of scientific instruments and a crucible boiling on a furnace.

evidence.quote:
we always keep a strongly charged
battery, ready for that purpose.
evidence.paraphrase: The old gentleman explains they keep a charged battery ready to deliver electric shocks.

evidence.quote:
his nativity had been carefully cast, and he would expire at exactly
thirty-five minutes, twenty-seven seconds, and five-sixths of a second
past nine o
clock, a.m., on that day two months.
evidence.paraphrase: The astrologers claim to have precisely calculated the exact moment of Tom's death.

evidence.quote:
all of a sudden, gentlemen, the crucible
blows up, with a great crash; everybody screams; the room is filled with
smoke
evidence.paraphrase: The crucible for the philosopher's stone explodes violently, filling the room with smoke.

evidence.quote:
this
same philosopher
s stone would have been discovered a hundred times at
least, to speak within bounds, if it wasn
t for the one unfortunate
circumstance that the apparatus always blows up, when it
s on the very
point of succeeding.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator claims the philosopher's stone would have been discovered many times but for the apparatus always exploding at the last moment.

evidence.quote:
the old gentleman wetted the forefinger of his right
hand in some of the liquor from the crucible that was spilt on the floor,
and drew a small triangle on Tom
s forehead.  The room swam before his
eyes, and he found himself in the watch-house.
evidence.paraphrase: After a mark is drawn on his forehead, Tom is suddenly transported back to the watch-house.

evidence.quote:
It was late at night, and he
found himself in the very watch-house from which he had been let out that
morning.
evidence.paraphrase: The ending reveals Tom is back where he started, suggesting the whole adventure may have been enchantment or fantasy.
